tagline.text: A small volcanic hill park in Legazpi with a full view of Mayon Volcano

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Bogtong, Legazpi City, Albay, about 3 km west of the city center

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–700 (per person, covering entrance, transport and an optional zipline)

children.text: Ligñon Hill is an old volcanic hill about 156 m high just west of downtown Legazpi, and its summit viewpoint takes in Mayon Volcano and Albay Gulf at a glance. With a wartime tunnel, a zipline and a volcano observatory, it fits neatly into a half-day Legazpi itinerary.
Ligñon Hill rises in Barangay Bogtong, Legazpi City, about
3 km
west of the downtown port area. It stands roughly
(512 ft) high and is known as a prehistoric cinder cone at the foot of Mayon Volcano, about
12 km

south-southeast of the volcano's summit. Its rock is mainly basaltic volcanic rock (dolerite). From the top you see Mayon's perfect cone to the northwest and Legazpi's cityscape and Albay Gulf to the east and south, which makes it the first viewpoint on many Legazpi itineraries.
Several layers of interest are stacked on this hill. The PHIVOLCS Mayon Volcano Observatory, built in 1989, is here, and a roughly

L-shaped tunnel dug by Japanese forces in World War II remains (some sources say 50 feet). A 2006 redevelopment added a viewing deck with coin-operated telescopes, a promenade, restaurants, souvenir shops and a zipline. Some sources say the city and provincial governments manage the park together, while others say the Albay provincial government runs it, and it is under redevelopment, so some facilities may be closed (visitor reviews from late 2025 mention summit facilities being shut or under renovation). Opening hours are listed from early morning until night depending on the source, and one guide says the morning hours are open free of charge to local joggers.

The hill's main advantage for travelers is how easy it is to reach. It lies between the airport and downtown, so you can squeeze in a visit on arrival or departure day, and the view is best in the early morning after the clouds clear from Mayon and around sunset. One guide says the last stretch to the viewing deck is a steep paved climb of about
20 minutes

on foot, and tricycles reportedly go only as far as the foot of the climb. This guide is for travelers staying in Legazpi who plan a day with Cagsawa Ruins and Daraga Church, and because fees and hours differ by source, check them locally.

Many travelers want to see Mayon up close, but access can be restricted when the volcano is active. Even then, Ligñon Hill offers a safe vantage point from which to see Mayon along with the rice fields and villages below it in a single scene. Because traces of eruptions and everyday life share one view, photographers may want to climb twice, once in the morning and once in the evening. On rainy or heavily clouded days, you can change plans and keep to a short visit to the tunnel and observatory. Mayon is one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines, and its perfect cone makes it a symbol of the Bicol region.
From the summit viewing deck you can see Mayon Volcano straight ahead to the northwest. On clear early mornings, local guidance says the cone looks sharpest around
. Clouds can hide it depending on the weather, so allow plenty of time at the top.

To the south and east, the view stretches across Legazpi's cityscape, Albay Gulf and neighboring Daraga. At dusk, when the city lights come on, the night view is worth seeing too. Coin-operated telescopes are installed for a closer look.
This L-shaped tunnel, about
long, was dug by Japanese forces in World War II. Local guides run tours explaining its wartime history, and safety helmets are provided. It is dark inside, so bring a flashlight.

You can try a zipline and rappelling near the summit. Older guides listed the basic zipline at ₱250 and the "Superman" style at ₱350, but current prices and whether it is operating may differ. It may stop running during redevelopment, so check on site.
Trails known as Burok-Burok, Kapit Tuko and Wisdom are listed for walking and hiking. An older guide says the walk to the viewpoint takes about
45 minutes to 1 hour
, so choose a route to suit your fitness and the weather.
The PHIVOLCS Mayon Volcano Observatory, built in 1989, sits on this hill and is described as doubling as a science house for visitors. Group tours are arranged by emailing PHIVOLCS.
Lonely Planet listed a hanging bridge (₱300), but prices and operation can change. A landscaped promenade, restaurants and souvenir shops make it pleasant to walk slowly and rest.

After sunset, lights come on across Legazpi and Daraga and Mayon's silhouette remains against the sky. Night operating hours differ by source, so confirm on site before going up and decide on your ride back in advance.
Take a Grab or tricycle from your hotel to the park entrance. One guide says vehicle entry is restricted in the early morning, so be ready to walk up from the entrance.
Walk up to the summit deck and watch the sun rise over Mayon Volcano.
Take photos as the clouds clear and look over the city through the coin-operated telescopes.
Tour the Japanese tunnel with a guide. Check that you have a helmet and a flashlight.
If activities such as the zipline are open, try them, then head back down to town for a late breakfast or early lunch.
Back in town, have a regional dish such as Bicol Express or laing for lunch and rest.
The climb takes about
20 minutes
but is steep, so water and comfortable shoes are essential.

items.title: Full Legazpi day
items.subtitle: Ligñon Hill and the Daraga area

children.text: Watch the sunrise and the Mayon Volcano view from Ligñon Hill.
Visit Cagsawa Ruins and Daraga Church in turn.
Have lunch in town with Bicolano dishes.
Go back up Ligñon Hill, enjoy the view at dusk, and come back down.
Domestic flights run from Manila to Bicol International Airport (DRP) in Daraga. Airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
From the airport, reach the city and the park by Grab, taxi or tricycle. Check fares locally.
The park is fairly close to the airport by car, but travel time depends on traffic, so check locally.
The airport and Ligñon Hill are both in the Legazpi–Daraga area, so it is easy to make a short visit on the day you arrive.
Long-distance buses run from Manila to Legazpi, and they commonly travel overnight and arrive the next morning. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so check with the bus company.
One guide advises taking a jeepney marked "Legazpi-Daraga Loop 1" and asking the driver to drop you near the park.
You can also go to the park entrance by tricycle or Grab. One guide says the final climb to the summit deck must be done on foot.

Ligñon Hill is worth most when the view is clear, so the dry season, when there is little rain and Mayon is sharp, is best. During the day, early morning with few clouds gives the best view, and sunset and the night view are also popular.
In the rainy and typhoon seasons, clouds and mist often hide Mayon and the climb is slippery. Bicol lies in the path of typhoons, so always check the weather forecast before your trip.

Weekends and holidays bring more local families, and afternoons tend to be crowded, so for a relaxed visit choose an early weekday morning. Hours may change during events and holidays, so check the latest notice.

Most lodging is clustered in downtown Legazpi and near the port rather than at Ligñon Hill, so it is usual to stay in town and travel back and forth. To see the sunrise, arrange your Grab pickup time the evening before. Check hotel and restaurant prices locally. A hotel close to the airport makes a short morning visit easy on arrival or departure day. For a sunrise outing, it is better to eat breakfast in town after you come down.

The park has restaurants and souvenir shops for simple meals and drinks. Signature Bicol dishes are Bicol Express (pork or other meat with coconut milk and hot chili), laing (taro leaves in coconut milk) and pinangat (taro leaf parcels). Look for local restaurants in town to try them.
Mayon is seen best on early mornings with few clouds. If it is cloudy, try again at dawn the next day.
The climb is steep, so bring non-slip shoes, water and a hat.
It is dark inside the tunnel, so a separate flashlight is easier to use than a phone light.
Take your trash with you. Smoking, drinking and picking flowers are reportedly prohibited.
Guides say knives and bolos may be confiscated at the entrance, so do not bring them.
Fees and hours differ by source, so check the latest information at the entrance.
Combining it with Cagsawa Ruins, Daraga Church and Sumlang Lake makes a full day.
The summit deck can be windy, so a thin jacket helps at dawn.
Clouds move fast, so take one photo as soon as you arrive and wait for a better moment afterward.
Bring plenty of cash. Entrance and activity fees may not accept cards.
Bicol is exposed to typhoons and Mayon's volcanic activity. Check the volcano alert level and the weather, and follow any access restrictions set by the authorities.
Redevelopment means the zipline and some facilities may be closed. Check local notices before building your plans around them.
The summit climb is steep and slippery in the rain. Children and older travelers should not push themselves.
The tunnel is dark with uneven ground, so wear the helmet and follow your guide.
It can be quiet at dawn and at night, so go with a companion rather than alone.
Fees and operating information here include older sources, so verify them again locally.
